+//! Bucket-based length padding for encrypted plaintexts.
+//!
+//! Both kind:445 group messages (MIP-03) and gift-wrapped Welcome events
+//! (MIP-02) historically leaked information through their on-the-wire size:
+//!
+//! - SelfRemove proposals are empty `MlsMessage::PublicMessage`s and stand out
+//!   as the smallest possible kind:445 events (issue #37).
+//! - Welcomes carry the full MLS ratchet tree, so the encrypted gift-wrap size
+//!   scales with the group's member count (issue #33).
+//!
+//! Padding the plaintext to a power-of-two bucket before encryption maps every
+//! plaintext into one of a small number of length classes, so a relay observer
+//! cannot distinguish messages within the same bucket.
+//!
+//! Padding is appended as zero bytes. The on-the-wire MLS framing uses TLS
+//! length-prefixed encoding, so the decoder consumes exactly the framed
+//! message and the trailing zero bytes are ignored. The deserialization sites
+//! that depend on this property are `process_mls_message` in
+//! `crate::messages::process` and `process_welcome` in [`crate::welcomes`].
+
+/// Minimum bucket size for kind:445 group message plaintexts.
+///
+/// Chosen so that the smallest possible MLS message (an empty SelfRemove
+/// `PublicMessage`) and a typical short text message land in the same bucket.
+/// A bare text rumor — pubkey, kind, created_at, id, sig, plus a few-byte
+/// `content` — already serializes to ~280 bytes of MLS `PrivateMessage`
+/// plaintext, so a 256-byte floor would leave SelfRemove proposals
+/// distinguishable. 512 bytes absorbs both classes.
+///
+/// Guards marmot-security issue #37 (SelfRemove size fingerprinting).
+pub(crate) const MESSAGE_PADDING_FLOOR: usize = 512;
+
+/// Minimum bucket size for the Welcome rumor payload (raw MLS bytes, before
+/// base64 encoding and NIP-59 gift wrapping).
+///
+/// Welcomes always carry the full ratchet tree, so they are inherently larger
+/// than chat messages; a higher floor keeps tiny groups indistinguishable from
+/// each other.
+pub(crate) const WELCOME_PADDING_FLOOR: usize = 1024;

_⚠️ Potential issue_ | _🟡 Minor_ | _⚡ Quick win_

**Guarantee these tests mutate trailing padding, not framed MLS bytes.**

At Line 8828 and Line 8982, the helper assumes the last byte is padding. If the serialized MLS message or Welcome already lands exactly on a bucket boundary, these branches flip real framed bytes instead, so the test can pass/fail for the wrong reason instead of isolating the zero-padding check.



<details>
<summary>🧪 Proposed fix</summary>

```diff
-                let target = serialized.len().next_power_of_two().max(512);
-                serialized.resize(target, 0);
-                *serialized.last_mut().expect("padded buffer is non-empty") = tail_byte;
+                serialized.push(tail_byte);
```

```diff
-                assert!(decoded.len() >= WELCOME_PADDING_FLOOR);
-                *decoded.last_mut().expect("decoded buffer non-empty") = tail_byte;
+                assert!(decoded.len() >= WELCOME_PADDING_FLOOR);
+                decoded.push(tail_byte);
```
</details>


Also applies to: 8978-8983

<details>
<summary>🤖 Prompt for AI Agents</summary>

```
Verify each finding against current code. Fix only still-valid issues, skip the
rest with a brief reason, keep changes minimal, and validate.

In `@crates/mdk-core/src/groups.rs` around lines 8826 - 8830, The test currently
assumes the last byte after resizing is padding, but if serialized.len() already
equals the bucket (power-of-two) size the resize is a no-op and you mutate real
framed bytes; before resizing compute target =
serialized.len().next_power_of_two().max(512) and if target == serialized.len()
bump target (e.g., target *= 2) to guarantee you expand the buffer, then call
serialized.resize(target, 0) and set *serialized.last_mut() = tail_byte; apply
the same change to both places that call serialized.resize(...) followed by
*serialized.last_mut() (the two occurrences that manipulate serialized and
tail_byte).
```

</details>

This one is interesting:

> The doc says the welcome floor was chosen so "tiny groups [are] indistinguishable from each other", but the test that validates this (`test_welcome_rumor_size_is_bucketed_for_small_groups`) only compares 1-member vs. 3-member welcomes — and only inside a single `mdk` instance with `MdkMemoryStorage`. OpenMLS Welcomes carry the ratchet tree + per-recipient HPKE-encrypted GroupSecrets, so a 5-member welcome will be substantially larger than a 1-member welcome and may cross the 1024→2048 boundary, defeating the privacy claim for the "small groups" cohort.
> 
> **Two options, pick one:**
> 
> - **Raise the floor** to something like `4096` (or `8192`) so realistic small-to-medium groups all land in the same bucket. The constant-factor cost on disk/wire is negligible compared to a kind:1059 gift-wrap and pays off in privacy.
> - **Tighten the test claim**: change the bullet in `padding.rs:48` from "tiny groups indistinguishable from each other" to "a single-member welcome is indistinguishable from an empty-payload welcome", and add a test that asserts the 1-member welcome length still fits in 1024 (so a future OpenMLS change that grows the welcome breaks the test loudly).
> 
> Either way, the current test only proves a property at *exactly* 1 vs 3 members in one cipher suite — it's a property the author should pick a number for, not measure once.

I think we should measure and understand exactly when groups start becoming distinguishable. And perhaps decide the padding based on how much uniformity we want vs extra size for small groups.

issue.title: fix: pad kind:445 and Welcome plaintexts to fixed-size buckets (sec #33, #37)
issue.body:
![marmot](https://blossom.primal.net/b9ff3ce9303fd9976e4da9b3a0740dfb71832b3f67ed4feae662f321be17d406.jpg)

## What this fixes

Two MEDIUM-severity metadata-leakage findings from the opus_vulns.md spec review:

- [marmot-security#33](https://github.com/marmot-protocol/marmot-security/issues/33): the encrypted size of a NIP-59 gift-wrapped Welcome event scales with the MLS ratchet tree, so a relay sees roughly how large the group is at invite time.
- [marmot-security#37](https://github.com/marmot-protocol/marmot-security/issues/37): empty SelfRemove `PublicMessage`s are the smallest possible kind:445 events. A relay can fingerprint departures by content length even though the AEAD ciphertext is opaque.

Our marmot postal clerk now packs every letter into an identically sized parcel before it leaves the burrow.

## What changes on the wire

Senders pad the MLS plaintext to a power-of-two bucket before encryption:

- **kind:445 messages**: floor 512 bytes, then round up to the next power of two. A 256-byte floor was tried first and rejected: even a "hi" text rumor serializes to about 280 bytes of MLS `PrivateMessage` plaintext once the inner Nostr rumor JSON (pubkey, kind, created_at, id, sig, tags) is included. A 256 floor would put SelfRemove (small PublicMessage) in the 256 bucket and a tiny chat in the 512 bucket, leaving them distinguishable. 512 collapses both into one bucket.
- **Welcome rumors**: floor 1024 bytes, then round up to the next power of two. Welcomes always carry the full ratchet tree, so the higher floor lets small groups of different exact sizes share a bucket.

Padding is appended as zero bytes. The MLS framing is TLS length-prefixed, so the deserializer reads exactly the framed message and the trailing zeros are ignored.

## Receiver changes

`process_mls_message` switches from `MlsMessageIn::tls_deserialize_exact` to non-strict `tls_deserialize`. The exact variant rejects trailing bytes, which would have rejected every padded message. Non-strict reads the framed message and stops, ignoring the padding. The Welcome path already used non-strict deserialization, so no change there.

Legacy unpadded messages still decode under the new receiver. There is a test for this.

## Compatibility note (Breaking)

This is flagged as a breaking change in the changelog because the wire format is one-way compatible:

- New receiver accepts new (padded) AND old (unpadded) messages.
- Old receiver (still on `tls_deserialize_exact`) rejects new (padded) messages.

All clients on the network need to upgrade. Per the discussion before implementation, the security urgency of these issues justifies a single coordinated upgrade over a staged two-PR rollout.

## Test evidence

461 mdk-core lib tests pass (450 pre-existing + 11 new):

- 7 unit tests in `padding.rs` covering bucket boundaries, floor behavior, and the zero-byte tail.
- 4 integration tests in `groups.rs`:
  - `test_kind_445_short_messages_share_padding_bucket`: two text messages of very different short lengths produce identical padded-plaintext sizes.
  - `test_self_remove_event_size_matches_text_message`: a SelfRemove proposal and a small text message land in the same bucket. This is the direct issue-#37 regression guard.
  - `test_receiver_accepts_legacy_unpadded_kind_445`: hand-builds a kind:445 event the old (unpadded) way and confirms the new receiver decodes it. Pins the forward-compatibility direction.
  - `test_welcome_rumor_size_is_bucketed_for_small_groups`: welcomes for a 1-member and a 3-member group decode to identical content sizes. This is the direct issue-#33 regression guard.

`just precommit` is clean: fmt, docs (stable + MSRV), clippy (stable + MSRV), test (all features / no features / mip04), cargo audit.

## Files touched

| File | Change |
| --- | --- |
| `crates/mdk-core/src/padding.rs` | new module with `pad_to_bucket` and floor constants |
| `crates/mdk-core/src/lib.rs` | declare the private `padding` module |
| `crates/mdk-core/src/groups.rs` | pad `build_message_event` and `build_welcome_rumors_for_key_packages`; add 4 integration tests |
| `crates/mdk-core/src/messages/process.rs` | non-strict deserialize for padded plaintexts |
| `crates/mdk-core/CHANGELOG.md` | Breaking-change + Fixed entries citing both issues |

Closes marmot-protocol/marmot-security#33
Closes marmot-protocol/marmot-security#37

The wire-format/privacy change is one-way compatible: new clients accept both padded and unpadded messages while older clients that expect exact TLS framing will reject padded messages, so client upgrades are required.

What changed:

![marmot](https://blossom.primal.net/b9ff3ce9303fd9976e4da9b3a0740dfb71832b3f67ed4feae662f321be17d406.jpg)

## What this fixes

Two MEDIUM-severity metadata-leakage findings from the opus_vulns.md spec review:

- [marmot-security#33](https://github.com/marmot-protocol/marmot-security/issues/33): the encrypted size of a NIP-59 gift-wrapped Welcome event scales with the MLS ratchet tree, so a relay sees roughly how large the group is at invite time.
- [marmot-security#37](https://github.com/marmot-protocol/marmot-security/issues/37): empty SelfRemove `PublicMessage`s are the smallest possible kind:445 events. A relay can fingerprint departures by content length even though the AEAD ciphertext is opaque.

Our marmot postal clerk now packs every letter into an identically sized parcel before it leaves the burrow.

## What changes on the wire

Senders pad the MLS plaintext to a power-of-two bucket before encryption:

- **kind:445 messages**: floor 512 bytes, then round up to the next power of two. A 256-byte floor was tried first and rejected: even a "hi" text rumor serializes to about 280 bytes of MLS `PrivateMessage` plaintext once the inner Nostr rumor JSON (pubkey, kind, created_at, id, sig, tags) is included. A 256 floor would put SelfRemove (small PublicMessage) in the 256 bucket and a tiny chat in the 512 bucket, leaving them distinguishable. 512 collapses both into one bucket.
- **Welcome rumors**: floor 1024 bytes, then round up to the next power of two. Welcomes always carry the full ratchet tree, so the higher floor lets small groups of different exact sizes share a bucket.

Padding is appended as zero bytes. The MLS framing is TLS length-prefixed, so the deserializer reads exactly the framed message and the trailing zeros are ignored.

## Receiver changes

`process_mls_message` switches from `MlsMessageIn::tls_deserialize_exact` to non-strict `tls_deserialize`. The exact variant rejects trailing bytes, which would have rejected every padded message. Non-strict reads the framed message and stops, ignoring the padding. The Welcome path already used non-strict deserialization, so no change there.

Legacy unpadded messages still decode under the new receiver. There is a test for this.

## Compatibility note (Breaking)

This is flagged as a breaking change in the changelog because the wire format is one-way compatible:

- New receiver accepts new (padded) AND old (unpadded) messages.
- Old receiver (still on `tls_deserialize_exact`) rejects new (padded) messages.

All clients on the network need to upgrade. Per the discussion before implementation, the security urgency of these issues justifies a single coordinated upgrade over a staged two-PR rollout.

## Test evidence

461 mdk-core lib tests pass (450 pre-existing + 11 new):

- 7 unit tests in `padding.rs` covering bucket boundaries, floor behavior, and the zero-byte tail.

`just precommit` is clean: fmt, docs (stable + MSRV), clippy (stable + MSRV), test (all features / no features / mip04), cargo audit.

| File | Change |
| --- | --- |
| `crates/mdk-core/src/padding.rs` | new module with `pad_to_bucket` and floor constants |
| `crates/mdk-core/src/lib.rs` | declare the private `padding` module |
| `crates/mdk-core/src/groups.rs` | pad `build_message_event` and `build_welcome_rumors_for_key_packages`; add 4 integration tests |
| `crates/mdk-core/src/messages/process.rs` | non-strict deserialize for padded plaintexts |

When a welcome arrives malformed, the colony was scribbling raw `{:?}`-formatted error strings into `ProcessedWelcome::failure_reason` and re-emitting them through `Error::Welcome` and the `tracing` log. Two problems followed:

- **Unbounded storage.** Both backends accepted `Option<String>` with no length cap, so an attacker who can influence the value gets a durable, unbounded sink in the marmot's own pantry.

The fix sanitizes at the source so we only ever write stable category strings, and caps at the storage layer so a future sloppy caller still can't blow up the pantry.

`crates/mdk-core/src/welcomes.rs::preview_welcome` had three sites that built `format!("...{:?}", e)` strings. Step 2 of 3: splitting #253. Part 1 (#258) landed the v3 wire format and storage column. This PR adds validation, the NIP-40 expiration tag, and the UniFFI surface. Part 3 handles deletion.

## What changed

**Validation.** `create_group` and `update_group_data` reject `Some(0)` with `Error::Group`. Callers pass `None` (or `Some(None)` on the update path) to disable. The extension constructor keeps its silent zero filter as a backstop; surfaced errors live at the public API where callers can act on them.

**NIP-40 expiration on outer wrappers.** `build_message_event` builds every outer kind:445 event: messages, proposals, commits. When the group has a `disappearing_message_secs` setting, the wrapper now carries an `expiration` tag. If the caller also supplies one (say, an ephemeral location burst), the earlier of the two wins. Group sets a ceiling; caller can ask for shorter but never longer. Both `created_at` and the expiration math share one `Timestamp::now()` snapshot so they cannot drift.

**UniFFI surface.** The `Group` record now exposes `disappearing_message_secs: Option<UInt64>`. On `GroupDataUpdate`, the field is `Option<Option<UInt64>>` (outer = specified, inner = enabled). For `create_group`, the binding takes a new `disappearing_message_secs` parameter. Mobile clients can read and write the duration through the binding now that the field is plumbed on both sides.

- Local message deletion methods (Part 3)
- UniFFI deletion exports (Part 3)
- `PRAGMA secure_delete=ON` (Part 3)

If you'd rather skip all updates until the next major or minor version, let me know by commenting `@dependabot ignore this major version` or `@dependabot ignore this minor version`. You can also ignore all major, minor, or patch releases for a dependency by adding an [`ignore` condition](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/supply-chain-security/configuration-options-for-dependency-updates#ignore) with the desired `update_types` to your config file.

If you change your mind, just re-open this PR and I'll resolve any conflicts on it.
